I'm tracing how user settings get created and propagated: they're set up on user creation via an after_create callback, exported users carry their own settings records, and placeholders lose their settings when destroyed since they're dependent. With bulk imports via insert_all, callbacks are skipped so settings aren't auto-created—they instead come from the exported User::Settings data, meaning if an imported user isn't in the export the placeholder just retains its original settings, and I'm considering the edge case where an exported user is missing settings entirely, which could break the timezone delegation.

For entropy records, the account's entropy already exists since it's created after_create, so for exported account-level entropy I need to update the existing record's auto_postpone_period while preserving its id, whereas board-level entropies can just be inserted normally. I'm also checking that the polymorphic container_id for Account-type entropy correctly maps to the new account id, and verifying the after_commit touch_all callback on cards won't cause issues since cards don't exist yet at that point in the import order. Now I'm working out which columns across tables reference the old account id and need remapping to the new account id during import.

Beyond entropy, I'm considering other account-referencing tables like account_cancellations and storage_totals that aren't exported, concluding Entropy is likely the main special case, and planning a generic approach that remaps any belongs_to or polymorphic reference targeting Account to the new id. I'm also thinking through the implications of importing webhooks as-is—whether their URLs and signing secrets should remain active, whether this risks duplicate deliveries across accounts, and whether SSRF protections are enforced at delivery time rather than at record creation, which would make bulk-inserting them without validation safe.

I'm noting that get_compressed_data_offset is public, and checking how get_eocd_offset reads the tail of the file—likely just the last ~64KB. For the central directory read, pulling the whole range in one request could mean a large in-memory string for archives with many entries, which works but is memory-heavy.

ZipKit handles Zip64 automatically for large files or entry counts, and uses data descriptors by default when writing to non-seekable output, so the reader's central directory sizes should still come out correct.

Now I'm sketching a RandomAccess-style IO wrapper around a blob: it tracks position and size, implements seek/tell, and fills a buffer by calling the storage service's download_chunk with byte ranges as needed. I'm weighing whether byte_size is reliably accurate for blobs created via S3 versus ones uploaded directly by users.

For performance, I want to special-case the Disk service -- since it exposes path_for, I can just open the local file directly instead of streaming chunks, falling back to the chunked remote reader otherwise. I'm checking whether MirrorService also delegates path_for to its primary service (it does, along with download, download_chunk, exist?, and url), and now I need to verify which storage service the test environment actually uses.

module FixturesTestHelper
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  class_methods do
    def identify(label, column_type = :integer)
      if label.to_s.end_with?("_uuid")
        column_type = :uuid
        label = label.to_s.delete_suffix("_uuid")
      end

      # Rails passes :string for varchar columns, so handle both :uuid and :string
      return super(label, column_type) unless column_type.in?([ :uuid, :string ])
      generate_fixture_uuid(label)
    end

    private

    def generate_fixture_uuid(label)
      # Generate deterministic UUIDv7 for fixtures that sorts by fixture ID
      # This allows .first/.last to work as expected in tests
      # Use the same CRC32 algorithm as Rails' default fixture ID generation
      # so that UUIDs sort in the same order as integer IDs
      fixture_int = Zlib.crc32("fixtures/#{label}") % (2**30 - 1)

      # Translate the deterministic order into times in the past, so that records
      # created during test runs are also always newer than the fixtures.
      base_time = Time.utc(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
      timestamp = base_time + (fixture_int / 1000.0)

      uuid_v7_with_timestamp(timestamp, label)
    end

    def uuid_v7_with_timestamp(time, seed_string)
      # Generate UUIDv7 with custom timestamp and deterministic random bits
      # Format: 48-bit timestamp_ms | 12-bit sub_ms_precision | 4-bit version | 62-bit random

      time_ms = time.to_f * 1000
      timestamp_ms = time_ms.to_i

      # 48-bit timestamp (milliseconds since epoch)
      bytes = []
      bytes[0] = (timestamp_ms >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[1] = (timestamp_ms >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[2] = (timestamp_ms >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[3] = (timestamp_ms >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[4] = (timestamp_ms >> 8) & 0xff
      bytes[5] = timestamp_ms & 0xff

      # Use the 12-bit rand_a field for sub-millisecond precision
      # Extract fractional milliseconds and convert to 12-bit value (0-4095)
      # This gives us ~0.244 microsecond precision
      frac_ms = time_ms - timestamp_ms
      sub_ms_precision = (frac_ms * 4096).to_i & 0xfff

      # Derive deterministic "random" bits from seed_string for the remaining random bits
      hash = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(seed_string)

      # 12-bit sub-ms precision + 4-bit version (0111 for v7)
      bytes[6] = ((sub_ms_precision >> 8) & 0x0f) | 0x70  # version 7
      bytes[7] = sub_ms_precision & 0xff

      # 2-bit variant (10) + 62-bit random
      rand_b = hash[3...19].to_i(16) & ((2**62) - 1)
      bytes[8] = ((rand_b >> 56) & 0x3f) | 0x80  # variant 10
      bytes[9] = (rand_b >> 48) & 0xff
      bytes[10] = (rand_b >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[11] = (rand_b >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[12] = (rand_b >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[13] = (rand_b >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[14] = (rand_b >> 8) & 0xff
      bytes[15] = rand_b & 0xff

      # Format as UUID string and convert to base36 (25 chars)
      uuid = "%02x%02x%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x%02x%02x%02x%02x" % bytes
      ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid.hex_to_base36(uuid.delete("-"))
    end
  end
end

module FixturesTestHelper
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  class_methods do
    def identify(label, column_type = :integer)
      if label.to_s.end_with?("_uuid")
        column_type = :uuid
        label = label.to_s.delete_suffix("_uuid")
      end

      # Rails passes :string for varchar columns, so handle both :uuid and :string
      return super(label, column_type) unless column_type.in?([ :uuid, :string ])
      generate_fixture_uuid(label)
    end

    private

    def generate_fixture_uuid(label)
      # Generate deterministic UUIDv7 for fixtures that sorts by fixture ID
      # This allows .first/.last to work as expected in tests
      # Use the same CRC32 algorithm as Rails' default fixture ID generation
      # so that UUIDs sort in the same order as integer IDs
      fixture_int = Zlib.crc32("fixtures/#{label}") % (2**30 - 1)

      # Translate the deterministic order into times in the past, so that records
      # created during test runs are also always newer than the fixtures.
      base_time = Time.utc(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
      timestamp = base_time + (fixture_int / 1000.0)

      uuid_v7_with_timestamp(timestamp, label)
    end

    def uuid_v7_with_timestamp(time, seed_string)
      # Generate UUIDv7 with custom timestamp and deterministic random bits
      # Format: 48-bit timestamp_ms | 12-bit sub_ms_precision | 4-bit version | 62-bit random

      time_ms = time.to_f * 1000
      timestamp_ms = time_ms.to_i

      # 48-bit timestamp (milliseconds since epoch)
      bytes = []
      bytes[0] = (timestamp_ms >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[1] = (timestamp_ms >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[2] = (timestamp_ms >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[3] = (timestamp_ms >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[4] = (timestamp_ms >> 8) & 0xff
      bytes[5] = timestamp_ms & 0xff

      # Use the 12-bit rand_a field for sub-millisecond precision
      # Extract fractional milliseconds and convert to 12-bit value (0-4095)
      # This gives us ~0.244 microsecond precision
      frac_ms = time_ms - timestamp_ms
      sub_ms_precision = (frac_ms * 4096).to_i & 0xfff

      # Derive deterministic "random" bits from seed_string for the remaining random bits
      hash = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(seed_string)

      # 12-bit sub-ms precision + 4-bit version (0111 for v7)
      bytes[6] = ((sub_ms_precision >> 8) & 0x0f) | 0x70  # version 7
      bytes[7] = sub_ms_precision & 0xff

      # 2-bit variant (10) + 62-bit random
      rand_b = hash[3...19].to_i(16) & ((2**62) - 1)
      bytes[8] = ((rand_b >> 56) & 0x3f) | 0x80  # variant 10
      bytes[9] = (rand_b >> 48) & 0xff
      bytes[10] = (rand_b >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[11] = (rand_b >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[12] = (rand_b >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[13] = (rand_b >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[14] = (rand_b >> 8) & 0xff
      bytes[15] = rand_b & 0xff

      # Format as UUID string and convert to base36 (25 chars)
      uuid = "%02x%02x%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x%02x%02x%02x%02x" % bytes
      ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid.hex_to_base36(uuid.delete("-"))
    end
  end
end

        base_scope
          .where(record_id: batch_ids)
          .joins(:blob)
          .sum("active_storage_blobs.byte_size")
      end
    end

In finalize I'll enqueue the reconcile job per account and per board. I should also check how the account seeder and name generator work for signup, plus how Current.identity behaves in the controller. Then I want to plan the user-visible export section in account settings, letting admins download everything in the account—boards, cards, comments, files, and people.

I'm sketching the rest of the export/import flow: a button posting to the account exports path with a flash notice, a profile page section letting users export just the cards they can see, and download pages that show "ready," "still preparing," or "link expired" states depending on export status. I'm also planning an imports page with a file upload form that creates a new account, plus an import show page that reports processing, completed, or failed states by email.

For the tenanted import show page, I'm realizing that if the import fails and the account gets destroyed, the page becomes inaccessible, which seems acceptable since it just redirects. There's a trickier issue though: if other imported users log in while the import is only partially done, they could start creating content in a half-finished account that later gets wiped on failure. To avoid that, I'm considering linking user identities only at the very end of the import process rather than as users are created, so nobody can access the account until it's fully finalized—inserting users with a null identity during import and linking identities only in a finalize step.

For the importer's own user and the system user, I'm thinking the same deferred-linking approach applies: keep the placeholder user active during import for continued access, then in finalize, destroy the placeholder and link the real exported user (with owner role) to the importer's identity. The system user needs similar handling—there'd temporarily be two system users during import, and finalize should destroy the placeholder one, though I need to check whether anything references that placeholder system user via associations during the import window.

Then I realize there's a concern: the recurring auto-postpone job runs globally across all accounts, so it could act on imported cards mid-import using the system user before finalize happens. On reflection this seems consistent with existing behavior, since the source instance would have already postponed any sufficiently stale cards itself.

But there's a race condition I need to flag: if the job runs between Card insertion and NotNow/Closure insertion, it could create a conflicting NotNow record for a card whose closure hasn't been imported yet, causing a unique index violation when the real card_not_nows data is imported later. For long-running imports spanning hours, this is a real risk, so I'm thinking about mitigations like flagging the account as "importing" so background jobs skip it entirely until finalize.

I'm also now worried about Notification::Bundle.deliver_all_later -- imported bundles with pending status and a past ends_at could get picked up and trigger real emails sent to imported users about old historical notifications, which would be a serious bug.

  "output": "class Notification::Bundle < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :account, default: -> { user.account }
  belongs_to :user

  enum :status, %i[ pending processing delivered ]

  scope :due, -> { pending.where("ends_at <= ?", Time.current) }
  scope :containing, ->(notification) { where("starts_at <= ? AND ends_at > ?", notification.updated_at, notification.updated_at) }
  scope :overlapping_with, ->(other_bundle) do
    where(
      "(starts_at <= ? AND ends_at >= ?) OR (starts_at <= ? AND ends_at >= ?) OR (starts_at >= ? AND ends_at <= ?)",
      other_bundle.starts_at, other_bundle.starts_at,
      other_bundle.ends_at, other_bundle.ends_at,
      other_bundle.starts_at, other_bundle.ends_at
    )
  end

  before_validation :set_default_window, if: :new_record?

  validate :validate_no_overlapping

  class << self
    def deliver_all
      due.in_batches do |batch|
        jobs = batch.collect { DeliverJob.new(it) }
        ActiveJob.perform_all_later jobs
      end
    end

    def deliver_all_later
      DeliverAllJob.perform_later
    end
  end

  def notifications
    user.notifications.where(updated_at: window).unread
  end

  def deliver
    user.in_time_zone do
      Current.with_account(user.account) do
        processing!

        Notification::BundleMailer.notification(self).deliver if deliverable?

        delivered!
      end
    end
  end

  def deliver_later
    DeliverJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def flush
    update!(ends_at: Time.current)
    deliver_later
  end

  def set_default_window
    self.starts_at ||= Time.current
    self.ends_at ||= self.starts_at + user.settings.bundle_aggregation_period
  end

  private
    def window

messages.thinking:
I'm thinking through delivery logic: bundles require an active account plus unread notifications, settings, and verification. Since importing would link identities and risk delivering stale summary emails for old unread notifications, I want to mark pending/processing bundles as already delivered on import to avoid spamming users, possibly through a small custom record set or a generic pre-insert transform hook.

I'm considering whether to give the generic RecordSet a `prepare(data)` hook, or create a dedicated subclass for Notification::Bundle so imported bundles get force-marked delivered rather than resent. Separately, I'm worried about a race during import: since the importing account's own active cards may get auto-postponed before their closure/not_now records are restored, this could create conflicting NotNow records when the real ones are inserted later, causing import failures.

There's also a dangling reference problem—events created by the placeholder system user during import could be left pointing at a deleted user once that placeholder is destroyed at finalize. I'm weighing options to isolate importing accounts from these background processes, like filtering `auto_postpone_all_due` to skip accounts with an active `Account::Import`, versus restructuring the import itself so card state records are inserted atomically alongside their cards, though that's hard to do with the current record-set design.

Realistically, this race window only matters for large imports that overlap with the hourly auto-postpone job, and a failure there would roll back the whole import—bad for a big customer. I'm leaning toward adding an explicit "importing" guard on Account that other global jobs check, since I'm now realizing there could be other vulnerable processes too, like a daily job that deletes unused tags before their taggings exist.

I'm weighing cleanup options for a failed SaaS account creation — considering `account.incinerate`, which runs destroy-related callbacks but I need to check whether it also triggers the "account cancelled" email, which isn't appropriate here since this is a failed setup rather than a genuine cancellation.

For large partially-imported accounts, running full AR callback cascades through millions of rows would be too slow, so I'm planning to sweep-delete imported rows via `delete_all` in reverse manifest order first, then purge blob files, then incinerate the now-nearly-empty account. I need to make sure this bypass doesn't skip important cleanup — search records only exist after finalize, and storage/search clearing callbacks are account-level, so that should be fine; for blobs, deleting each blob also removes its variant files, and since variants are themselves blobs tied to the account, they're already covered by the account-level deletion.

I'm now worried about a safety edge case: if a crafted import zip reuses a blob key that already exists in another account, the unique index should reject the insert and fail the import before any file upload happens, so our cleanup (scoped to the new account's blob rows) wouldn't touch the other account's blob — but I need to confirm the upload step itself can't overwrite another account's file before the DB insert fails, since keys are guaranteed unique at the DB level before any upload proceeds.

I also want to check for path traversal in blob keys — something like "../../etc/passwd" could escape the storage root via `path_for`. Rails 7.1+'s DiskService raises `InvalidKeyError` for paths that escape root, but I should still consider validating blob keys strictly against the expected `base36` format used by ActiveStorage, since variants, previews, or legacy data might contain unexpected key formats.

I also need to think about the zip entry path convention (storage/<key>) and how service_name and checksum verification should work on upload—using the service's checksum validation to catch corrupted files, keeping in mind that checksum formats differ between Disk (base64 md5) and S3 (possibly sha256-prefixed) services, so cross-service imports need careful handling.

I also need to parse a checksum prefix — none means MD5, "sha256:" means SHA256 — and skip verification otherwise. On top of that I need to verify written byte_size matches the blob's recorded size, capping reads at byte_size+1 to catch bombs, and decide how to handle blobs whose files are missing from the zip since exports skip missing files.

For writing the zip, I should check file existence before starting the entry to avoid leaving a corrupt partial entry if download raises FileNotFoundError mid-stream.

messages.thinking:
I'm creating two new migrations timestamped after the latest one, starting with an exports table that tracks account, user, type, and status fields with a pending default.

For account_imports I'm adding account and identity references, a status field, and considering whether to keep a failure_reason column — but since I've decided a failed import destroys the record entirely, that column would only hold data momentarily, which gives me pause. I'm also thinking through the edge case where a user lands on the tenanted import show page after upload, sees "Importing…", and the account gets deleted on failure before they refresh.

I'll drop the failure_reason column but still persist "failed" status before cleanup runs, so if cleanup itself crashes partway through, the record remains visible as failed for admins to inspect rather than vanishing silently. That gives a safer ordering: mark failed, send the notification email, then destroy everything — though I'm now weighing whether the email should fire before or after cleanup, since a slow cleanup delays the email, but a crashed cleanup after sending it means a user already notified sees a clean failure.

Since emails are enqueued asynchronously via deliver_later, sending before cleanup works fine regardless of cleanup duration. For the manifest validation, I confirm that the check phase verifies all referenced files exist in the zip before any inserts happen, so the order of record sets in the manifest doesn't actually matter.

Now I'm writing the ZipFile reader class with methods for reading entries and globbing filenames...

I realize glob performance will be a real problem at scale: with 40 record sets each calling glob against millions of entries using fnmatch, that's hundreds of millions of comparisons, taking minutes. I need to index entries by directory upfront, then optimize glob to do a direct directory lookup plus suffix filtering when the pattern has no wildcard in the directory portion, falling back to full fnmatch scanning otherwise.

I'm also weighing the memory cost of holding millions of ZipEntry objects — roughly 600MB-1.5GB depending on entry count — and considering whether to store only the essential fields (offset, sizes, storage mode) in compact arrays instead of full entry objects to keep memory usage down for a background worker.

Actually this per-entry read pattern worries me — each small JSON entry requires a GET for its local header plus another for its data, so with 2 million records that's 4 million S3 requests, which at roughly 20ms each would take about 22 hours. Way too slow. I need a read-ahead buffering strategy instead, relying on the fact that entries are stored sequentially in the zip in the same order they were exported, since records are fetched via find_each ordered by primary key and base36 ids with fixed length sort lexicographically the same as numerically.

So I'm designing a RemoteIO class with an 8MB read-ahead buffer: on each read request, serve from the buffer if the position is covered, otherwise fetch a larger chunk starting at that position to minimize the total number of S3 GETs needed.

For large blob reads, local header reads, and both the check and import passes over the JSON data, this buffering strategy keeps things mostly sequential and efficient — though downloading an entire 500GB file to a temp disk via blob.open isn't feasible, so I need to stick with streaming reads instead.

I'll cap the max uncompressed size per JSON entry with a constant like MAX_RECORD_SIZE, since rich text bodies are rarely huge. ZipKit's reader handles data descriptors and Zip64 fine since it relies on the central directory's sizes.

Writing the Reader class's Entry struct...

For reading a single path, I'll look up the entry, enforce the size limit against uncompressed_size, then stream chunks into a buffer while double-checking the accumulated size doesn't exceed the limit as a safety net.

For the streaming method, I want it to yield chunks while guarding against decompression bombs by raising if the inflated size exceeds the declared uncompressed size. I'm also considering adding CRC32 verification during streaming since ZipKit doesn't do this itself — computing it as a cheap integrity check against corrupted archives seems worthwhile to add.

For error handling, I want to wrap ZipKit's internal exceptions (like missing EOCD or malformed structure errors) into my own ZipFile-specific error types, rescuing them in the Reader constructor and re-raising as something clearer for callers.

Now I'm sketching `ZipFile.read_from`, which opens an IO for a given blob and yields a Reader, closing the IO afterward. I need an `io_for` helper that checks whether the blob's storage service supports direct file paths (like Disk service) and opens the file directly if so, otherwise falling back to a remote IO wrapper. I'm also thinking through edge cases — what happens if the service's path points to a missing file, and how mirrored services might delegate path resolution.

I'll handle JSON serialization for records, pre-serializing times before encoding, then start building the RecordSet base class with its initializer accepting account, model, and attributes.

Adding export, check, and import methods...

I realize the check needs the exported account id for remapping account references, pulled from the zip's account.json and memoized. For import, account_id always maps to the current account.id, while other belongs_to references to Account need generic handling based on reflections.

Working out reference columns from reflections...

I'm building a check that verifies each record's foreign keys actually resolve, either via polymorphic type lookup or the reflection's class, raising an integrity error if the referenced row isn't found.

Now I need a way to map polymorphic type names to their model classes, which means figuring out where the manifest should expose its list of exportable models — I'm weighing whether to restructure the Manifest class to support a lookup like `model_for` given the current instance-based, account-scoped design.

I'm reconsidering the design to avoid hacky memoization—instead I want a clean class method on Manifest that can look up a model by its polymorphic name, built from a static list of record set models rather than instantiating repeatedly.

I'm thinking through how RecordSet can reference Manifest's models list to build an exportable models index keyed by polymorphic name, accounting for STI subclasses where the polymorphic name comes from the base class.

For conflict detection, I'm planning to batch-check record IDs against existing account data and raise a clear error naming the conflicting model type without exposing details, while noting duplicate IDs within a single zip can't occur since the file index naturally dedupes entries.

Also need to verify imported IDs match filenames, and figure out how to handle required NOT NULL columns without defaults — I want to avoid hard failures when importing from older Fizzy exports missing newer columns, so I'm computing required attributes as those truly NOT NULL with no default or default function, excluding account_id and timestamp fields that insert_all handles automatically.

Unknown keys from newer exports are simply ignored via slicing, keeping backward compatibility, and I'm skipping value-type validation since the database will reject bad values anyway. Writing batch import logic...

But I realize `insert_all!` requires all rows to share identical keys, so if older exports lack optional columns the insert will fail—filling missing keys with nil would wrongly override DB defaults and trigger NOT NULL errors, so instead I should group rows by their key set and run `insert_all!` separately per group.

Now turning to the account record set: the export writes account attributes (id, name, cards_count, timestamps, possibly external_account_id) plus a join_code object with code, usage_count, usage_limit, and the file list is just the account.json path, with integrity checks confirming the file exists and contains "id" and "name". For import I'm thinking about updating the account's name and bumping cards_count to the max of imported vs current, then handling the join code's usage_limit update separately.

On the join code question, I decide to keep the account's own code and usage_count untouched but still import the exported usage_limit for consistency, since fully ignoring the join code data defeats the purpose of exporting it.

Next I move to the UserRecordSet: exporting users with email_address from identity, plus id, name, role, active, verified_at, and timestamps while excluding identity_id as instance-specific, and the check step needs to validate email format and enforce no duplicate emails across the batch.

I'm reasoning that duplicate detection during check needs a Set, even though resume offsets make it incomplete—acceptable since the DB's unique index will ultimately catch collisions when identities get linked during finalize. For import, I insert users with identity_id nil and keep roles as-is, since owner demotion/promotion logic belongs in finalize. I'm deciding where identity-linking logic should live — probably as a method on UserRecordSet itself, since it's fundamentally about users.

I'm now weighing whether linking identities should happen at the end of finalize versus during import — I lean toward finalize to avoid exposing partially-linked users mid-import. But that raises a concern: between insertion and finalize, imported users have no identity, so checking setup status could crash on a nil email address if anyone views the account mid-import, like through the users list page — I need to check whether the active users scope would even include these identity-less records.

For entropy records, I'm handling account-level vs board-level differently: account entropy updates the existing record's auto_postpone_period, while board entropy gets inserted fresh, with a polymorphic container-type check to distinguish them. For blob records, I'm exporting ActiveStorage blobs by account excluding internal ones, validating key format and checking for cross-account key conflicts, then adding the service_name attribute back in during import since it's excluded from the stored attributes.

Variant records just need a generic belongs_to blob reference check. For attachments, I'm excluding non-exportable record types during export, verifying both the record and its blob are present in the zip during check, and using a plain insert_all for import since attachments only have created_at timestamps -- though I need to remember this bypasses the normal attachment tracking callbacks, so I'll need to reconcile that state afterward, and the check phase already guards against cross-account blob reuse by requiring the blob to exist in the zip.

Now for RichText records: export converts sgids to gids in the body, and check needs to verify the record type is exportable and in the zip, plus validate every gid reference in the body points to an exportable model present in the zip. I'm weighing what to do about dangling references -- users are never truly destroyed so that's less of a concern, but purged blobs referenced in old text bodies are trickier, since sgid resolution would fail and I need to decide whether to leave the sgid unconverted or strip it during export.

On import, I'm thinking the safest approach is to strip gid references that don't resolve to a record in the zip rather than fail the import, since ActionText already handles missing attachables gracefully by rendering a placeholder. Real exports should only ever contain gids for records scoped to the same account, so a crafted zip referencing another account's blob would just get silently stripped, which seems like the safe and lenient behavior to settle on.

For sgids embedded in bodies, I'm leaning toward stripping all of them at import regardless since they're signed by another instance and can't be trusted or re-verified anyway — then I convert any valid gids into fresh sgids for the new instance. I also need to double check the gid format and how `GlobalID.app` is configured to make sure the generated gids match what the importer expects.

Now for file records, the approach is: export each blob by streaming its chunks into a zip entry under `storage/<key>`, skipping any blobs that are missing. For the check phase, instead of verifying nothing, I could compare each stored file's uncompressed size against the blob's `byte_size` field cheaply via the zip's central directory, raising an integrity error on mismatch. Import would then need to reconstruct each blob from its JSON record and corresponding file.

I'm figuring out how importing a blob's file works: stream it to a tempfile verifying size and checksum, then upload it through the correct storage service (resolved from the blob's `service_name`), only processing blobs that have a JSON record so stray zip entries can't be used to write arbitrary files. I'm also noting that variant image blobs are just regular blobs attached to a VariantRecord, so they'd follow the same file-handling path.

For Notification::Bundle, I'm considering a small subclass of the generic record set that marks status as delivered on import, placed at `account/data_transfer/notification_bundle_record_set.rb`. For events, I'm thinking about validating that `assignee_ids` in particulars reference users present in the zip — since users are rarely hard-deleted (deactivated accounts keep their user records), a strict existence check should be safe, though I want to confirm whether users can ever actually be destroyed.

Since identity destruction just deactivates rather than removing the user, I'll lean toward leniency: filtering out unknown IDs in a `prepare(data)` hook rather than failing the import outright. But I'm now worried about Filter records — since their HABTM join tables (assignees, tags, boards, creators, closers) aren't exported, an imported filter would lose those criteria while its `params_digest` still reflects the original params, meaning `find_by_params` could match it against the wrong, now-criteria-less filter when a user reapplies the same search.

cd /app && cat > app/models/zip_file.rb <<'EOF'
class ZipFile
  class Error < StandardError; end
  class InvalidFileError < Error; end
  class MissingEntryError < InvalidFileError; end

  class << self
    def create_for(attachment, filename:)
      raise ArgumentError, "No block given" unless block_given?

      reflection = attachment.record.class.reflect_on_attachment(attachment.name)
      service_name = reflection.options[:service_name] || ActiveStorage::Blob.service.name
      service = ActiveStorage::Blob.services.fetch(service_name)

      if s3_service?(service)
        create_for_s3(attachment, filename: filename, service: service) { |zip| yield zip }
      else
        create_for_disk(attachment, filename: filename) { |zip| yield zip }
      end
    end

    # Yields a ZipFile::Reader for the archive stored in +blob+. Archives on disk
    # are read in place; any other service is read with ranged requests, so the
    # archive never has to be downloaded as a whole.
    def read_from(blob)
      raise ArgumentError, "No block given" unless block_given?

      io = open_for_reading(blob)
      yield Reader.new(io)
    ensure
      io&.close
    end

    private
      def s3_service?(service)
        # The S3 service doesn't get loaded in development unless it's used
        defined?(ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service) && service.is_a?(ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service)
      end

      def disk_service?(service)
        defined?(ActiveStorage::Service::DiskService) && service.is_a?(ActiveStorage::Service::DiskService)
      end

      def create_for_s3(attachment, filename:, service:)
        blob = ActiveStorage::Blob.create_before_direct_upload!(
          filename: filename,
          content_type: "application/zip",
          byte_size: 0,
          checksum: "pending",
          service_name: service.name
        )

        writer = Writer.new

        # Use S3's upload_stream directly for write-based streaming.
        # ActiveStorage's upload method expects a read-based IO, but ZipKit
        # needs a write-based stream. The TransferManager's upload_stream
        # yields a writable IO that we can stream directly to.
        service.send(:upload_stream,
          key: blob.key,
          content_type: "application/zip",
          part_size: 100.megabytes
        ) do |write_stream|
          write_stream.binmode
          writer.stream_to(write_stream)
          yield writer
          writer.close
        end

        blob.update!(byte_size: writer.byte_size, checksum: writer.checksum)
        attachment.attach(blob)
      rescue Aws::S3::MultipartUploadError => e
        if e.errors.any?
          raise e.errors.first
        else
          raise e
        end
      end

      def create_for_disk(attachment, filename:)
        tempfile = Tempfile.new([ "export", ".zip" ])
        tempfile.binmode

        writer = Writer.new(tempfile)
        yield writer
        writer.close

I realize there's a bug in zip_kit 6.3.4 where num_files_in_archive counts fillers, so after a rollback the EOCD reports one extra entry than actually exists, causing strict readers to fail—and our import relies on ZipKit's strict reader. This means a failed blob download during export could trigger a rollback that corrupts the archive's entry count, so I need to avoid rollbacks entirely.

The safest approach is checking file existence before adding each entry rather than rescuing failures mid-download, since a race condition could still corrupt the EOCD if a file disappears partway through. If a download fails mid-entry, I should let the exception propagate and mark the whole export as failed rather than attempting a rollback—better to let the user retry than ship a corrupted zip.

A cleaner fix might be subclassing ZipKit's writer so the end-of-central-directory record counts actual central directory headers written instead of relying on a potentially inaccurate file count passed in. I'm sketching a custom ZipWriter subclass that overrides the EOCD-writing method to track this count internally.

Once that's set, I should rescue FileNotFoundError per-blob in exports so missing files are simply skipped, then implement and test the whole thing.

# Exports and imports the records of one model as JSON files in a ZIP archive,
# one file per record at data/<table name>/<id>.json.
#
# Imports keep the original ids so that every reference between records, rich
# text attachments and JSON columns survives the trip. Before anything gets
# inserted, +check+ makes sure that every reference points to a record from the
# same archive, so an import can never reach into data that belongs to another
# account.
class Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  class IntegrityError < StandardError; end
  class ConflictError < IntegrityError; end

  INTERNAL_RECORD_TYPES = %w[ Export Account::Import ].freeze
  BATCH_SIZE = 100
  MAX_RECORD_SIZE = 64.megabytes
  ACCOUNT_FILE = "data/account.json"

  attr_reader :account, :model, :attributes

  def initialize(account:, model:, attributes: nil)
    @account = account
    @model = model
    @attributes = (attributes || model.column_names).map(&:to_s)
  end

  def export(to:)
    with_zip(to) do
      records.find_each do |record|
        export_record(record)
      end
    end
  end

  # Validates the records in the archive without changing anything. Yields the
  # number of files checked so far after each batch, so callers can resume from
  # there with +start+.
  def check(from:, start: 0)
    with_zip(from) do
      each_batch_of_files(start: start) do |batch, checked|
        check_batch(batch)
        yield checked if block_given?
      end
    end
  end

  # Imports the records in the archive. Records that are already in the account
  # are skipped, so an interrupted import can be resumed or run again safely.
  def import(from:, start: 0)
    with_zip(from) do
      each_batch_of_files(start: start) do |batch, imported|
        import_batch(batch)
        yield imported if block_given?
      end
    end
  end

  def files
    zip.glob("data/#{model_dir}/*.json")
  end

  private
    attr_reader :zip

    def with_zip(zip)
      old_zip = @zip
      @zip = zip
      yield
    ensure
      @zip = old_zip
    end

    def records
      model.where(account_id: account.id)
    end

    def model_dir
      model.table_name
    end

    def export_record(record)
      zip.add_file(path_for(model, record.id), serialize(record).to_json)
    end

    def serialize(record)
      # Read raw attribute values: some models decorate their columns with
      # objects (like Column#color), which must not end up in the export.
      record.attributes.slice(*attributes).transform_values do |value|
        value.respond_to?(:utc) ? value.utc.iso8601(6) : value
      end
    end

    def each_batch_of_files(start:)
      start = start.to_i

      files.drop(start).each_slice(BATCH_SIZE).with_index do |batch, index|
        yield batch, start + (index * BATCH_SIZE) + batch.size
      end
    end

    def check_batch(batch)
      batch.each { |file| check_record(file, load(file)) }
      check_conflicts(batch.map { |file| File.basename(file, ".json") })
    end

    def check_record(file, data)
      unless data.is_a?(Hash) && data["id"].to_s == File.basename(file, ".json")
        raise IntegrityError, "#{file} doesn't match the record it contains"
      end

      if (missing = required_attributes - data.keys).any?
        raise IntegrityError, "#{file} is missing #{missing.to_sentence}"
      end

      check_references(file, data)
    end

    def required_attributes
      @required_attributes ||= model.columns.filter_map do |column|
        column.name if !column.null && column.default.nil? && column.default_function.nil?
      end - %w[ account_id created_at updated_at ] & attributes
    end

    def check_references(file, data)
      references.each do |reference|
        id = data[reference.foreign_key]

        if id.nil?
          raise IntegrityError, "#{file} is missing its #{reference.name}" unless reference.optional?
        elsif !referenced?(reference.target_for(data), id)
          raise IntegrityError, "#{file} refers to a #{reference.name} that isn't in the file"
        end
      end
    end

    def references
      @references ||= model.reflect_on_all_associations(:belongs_to).filter_map do |reflection|
        if reflection.foreign_key.to_s != "account_id" && attributes.include?(reflection.foreign_key.to_s)
          Reference.new(reflection, exportable_models)
        end
      end
    end

    def referenced?(target, id)
      if target.nil?
        false
      elsif target <= Account
        id == source_account_id
      else
        zip.exists?(path_for(target, id))
      end
    end

    def check_conflicts(ids)
      if records_elsewhere(ids).exists?
        raise ConflictError, "Some #{model.model_name.human.pluralize.downcase} in this file already exist in Fizzy"
      end
    end

    def records_elsewhere(ids)
      model.where(id: ids).where.not(account_id: account.id)
    end

    def import_batch(batch)
      rows = batch.filter_map { |file| prepare(load(file)) }
      existing_ids = model.where(id: rows.pluck("id")).pluck(:id).to_set

      insert rows.reject { |row| existing_ids.include?(row["id"]) }

# Lists everything that goes into an account export, in the order it has to be
# imported.
class Account::DataTransfer::Manifest
  attr_reader :account

  class << self
    # The models whose records can be in an export. Polymorphic references in

    def models
      @models ||= new(nil).send(:record_sets).map(&:model).uniq
    end
  end

    @account = account
  end

  # Yields each record set along with its position, starting from +start+ so
  # that an interrupted import can pick up where it left off.
  def each_record_set(start: 0)
    raise ArgumentError, "No block given" unless block_given?

    record_sets.each_with_index.drop(start.to_i).each do |record_set, index|
      yield record_set, index
    end
  end

class Account::DataTransfer::AccountRecordSet < Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  ATTRIBUTES = %w[ id name cards_count created_at updated_at ].freeze
  JOIN_CODE_ATTRIBUTES = %w[ code usage_count usage_limit ].freeze

  def initialize(account)
    super(account: account, model: Account, attributes: ATTRIBUTES)
  end

  def files
    if zip.exists?(ACCOUNT_FILE)
      [ ACCOUNT_FILE ]
    else
      raise IntegrityError, "This file isn't a Fizzy account export"
    end
  end

  private
    def records
      Account.where(id: account.id).includes(:join_code)
    end

    def export_record(account)
      zip.add_file ACCOUNT_FILE, serialize(account).merge("join_code" => account.join_code&.slice(*JOIN_CODE_ATTRIBUTES)).to_json
    end

    def check_record(file, data)
      unless data.is_a?(Hash) && data["id"].present? && data["name"].is_a?(String)
        raise IntegrityError, "This file isn't a Fizzy account export"
      end
    end

    # The account itself isn't inserted: the import goes into a new one.
    def check_conflicts(records)
    end

    def import_batch(batch)
      data = load(batch.first)

# Users are exported with the email address of their identity. Identities are
# global, so imported users are linked to them only once everything else is in
# place (see #link_identities): until then, nobody but the importer can get into
# an account that's still being imported.
class Account::DataTransfer::UserRecordSet < Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  ATTRIBUTES = %w[ id name role active verified_at created_at updated_at ].freeze

  def initialize(account)
    super(account: account, model: User, attributes: ATTRIBUTES)
  end

  # Links each imported user to the identity for their email address, creating
  # identities that don't exist yet. Users that were in the account before the
  # import and share an identity with an imported user are replaced by it.
  def link_identities(from:)
    with_zip(from) do
      each_exported_user do |data|
        if (identity = identity_for(data["email_address"]))
          account.users.where(identity: identity).where.not(id: data["id"]).destroy_all
          account.users.where(id: data["id"], identity_id: nil).update_all(identity_id: identity.id)
        end
      end
    end
  end

  def email_addresses(from:)
    with_zip(from) do
      [].tap do |email_addresses|
        each_exported_user { |data| email_addresses << data["email_address"] if data["email_address"].present? }
      end
    end
  end

  def exported?(user, from:)
    from.exists?(path_for(User, user.id))
  end

  private
    def records
      User.where(account: account).includes(:identity)
    end

    def serialize(user)
      super.merge("email_address" => user.identity&.email_address)
    end

    def check_record(file, data)
      super
      check_email_address(file, data["email_address"]) if data["email_address"].present?
    end

    def check_email_address(file, email_address)
      if !email_address.is_a?(String) || !email_address.match?(URI::MailTo::EMAIL_REGEXP)
        raise IntegrityError, "#{file} has an invalid email address"
      elsif !checked_email_addresses.add?(email_address.strip.downcase)
        raise IntegrityError, "More than one person in this file has the email address #{email_address}"
      end
    end

    def checked_email_addresses
      @checked_email_addresses ||= Set.new
    end

    def each_exported_user(&block)
      files.each { |file| block.call(load(file)) }
    end

    def identity_for(email_address)
      Identity.find_or_create_by!(email_address: email_address) if email_address.present?
    end
end

# Filters are exported along with the records they're narrowed down to, which
# live in join tables. Without them, a filter's digest would no longer match
# what it actually selects.
class Account::DataTransfer::FilterRecordSet < Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  RESOURCES = %i[ tags boards assignees creators closers ].freeze

  def initialize(account)
    super(account: account, model: Filter)
  end

  private
    def records
      super.includes(*RESOURCES.map { |resource| :"#{join_table_for(resource)}" })
    end

    def serialize(filter)
      super.merge RESOURCES.to_h { |resource| [ ids_key_for(resource), filter.public_send(ids_key_for(resource)) ] }
    end

    def import_batch(batch)
      exported_filters = batch.map { |file| load(file) }
      new_filter_ids = exported_filters.pluck("id") - Filter.where(id: exported_filters.pluck("id")).pluck(:id)
      new_filters = exported_filters.select { |data| data["id"].in?(new_filter_ids) }

      Filter.transaction do
        insert new_filters.map { |data| prepare(data) }
        RESOURCES.each { |resource| insert_resources(resource, new_filters) }
      end
    end

    def insert_resources(resource, filters)
      reflection = Filter.reflect_on_association(resource)

      rows = filters.flat_map do |data|
        Array(data[ids_key_for(resource)]).select { |id| zip.exists?(path_for(reflection.klass, id)) }.uniq.map do |id|
          { reflection.foreign_key => data["id"], reflection.association_foreign_key => id }
        end
      end

      join_model_for(resource).insert_all!(rows) if rows.any?
    end

    def ids_key_for(resource)
      "#{resource.to_s.singularize}_ids"
    end

    def join_table_for(resource)
      Filter.reflect_on_association(resource).join_table
    end

    def join_model_for(resource)
      Filter._reflect_on_association(join_table_for(resource)).klass
    end
end
EOF

class Account::DataTransfer::ActiveStorage::BlobRecordSet < Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  def initialize(account)
    super(
      account: account,
      model: ::ActiveStorage::Blob,
      attributes: ::ActiveStorage::Blob.column_names - %w[service_name]
    )
  end

  private
    def records
      ::ActiveStorage::Blob.where(account: account).where.not(id: excluded_blob_ids)
    end

    def excluded_blob_ids
      ::ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(account: account, record_type: INTERNAL_RECORD_TYPES).select(:blob_id)
    end

    def check_record(file, data)
      super
      raise IntegrityError, "#{file} has an invalid key" unless valid_key?(data["key"])
    end

    def valid_key?(key)
      key.is_a?(String) && key.split("/", -1).all? { |segment| segment.match?(/\A[\w\-.]+\z/) && !segment.in?(%w[ . .. ]) }
    end

    def check_conflicts(records)
      super

      if ::ActiveStorage::Blob.where(key: records.pluck("key")).where.not(account_id: account.id).exists?
        raise ConflictError, "Some files in this file already exist in this Fizzy, so it can't be imported again"
      end
    end

    # Files are uploaded to the storage service this Fizzy uses, whatever the
    # service they were exported from.
    def prepare(data)
      super.merge("service_name" => ::ActiveStorage::Blob.service.name)
    end
end

# The contents of the files behind every exported blob, stored uncompressed at
# storage/<blob key>.
class Account::DataTransfer::ActiveStorage::FileRecordSet < Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  def initialize(account)
    super(account: account, model: ::ActiveStorage::Blob)
  end

  private
    def records
      ::ActiveStorage::Blob.where(account: account).where.not(id: excluded_blob_ids)
    end

    def excluded_blob_ids
      ::ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(account: account, record_type: INTERNAL_RECORD_TYPES).select(:blob_id)
    end

    def export_record(blob)
      zip.add_file(storage_path(blob.key), compress: false) do |file|
        blob.download { |chunk| file.write(chunk) }
      end
    rescue ::ActiveStorage::FileNotFoundError
      # The file is gone from storage. The blob is still exported, like it is.
    end

    def check_batch(batch)
      batch.each do |file|
        data = load(file)
        path = storage_path(data["key"])

        if zip.exists?(path) && zip.size_of(path) != data["byte_size"].to_i
          raise IntegrityError, "#{data["filename"]} doesn't match its size in the file"
        end
      end
    end

    # Only files for blobs that were imported into the account get uploaded,
    # using the blob as it was stored rather than what the archive says.
    def import_batch(batch)
      blobs = ::ActiveStorage::Blob.where(account: account, id: batch.map { |file| File.basename(file, ".json") })

      blobs.each do |blob|
        upload(blob) if zip.exists?(storage_path(blob.key))
      end
    end

    def upload(blob)
      Tempfile.create([ "import", blob.filename.extension_with_delimiter ], binmode: true) do |file|
        digest = digest_for(blob.checksum)

        zip.stream(storage_path(blob.key)) do |chunk|
          file.write(chunk)
          digest&.update(chunk)
        end

        verify_integrity(blob, file, digest)

        file.rewind
        blob.service.upload(blob.key, file, content_type: blob.content_type)
      end
    end

    def digest_for(checksum)
      case checksum.to_s
      when /\Asha256:/ then OpenSSL::Digest::SHA256.new
      when /\A[A-Za-z0-9+\/]{22}==\z/ then OpenSSL::Digest::MD5.new
      end
    end

    def verify_integrity(blob, file, digest)
      if file.size != blob.byte_size || (digest && digest.base64digest != blob.checksum.delete_prefix("sha256:"))
        raise IntegrityError, "#{blob.filename} is corrupted"
      end
    end

    def storage_path(key)
      "storage/#{key}"
    end
end

# Attachments in rich text point to their records with signed global ids, which
# only the Fizzy that signed them can verify. They're exported as plain global
# ids, and signed again on import, but only for records imported into the same
# account.
class Account::DataTransfer::ActionText::RichTextRecordSet < Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  ATTACHMENT_SELECTOR = "action-text-attachment".freeze

  def initialize(account)
    super(account: account, model: ::ActionText::RichText)
  end

  private
    def records
      ::ActionText::RichText.where(account: account)
    end

    def serialize(rich_text)
      super.merge("body" => convert_sgids_to_gids(rich_text.body_before_type_cast))
    end

    def convert_sgids_to_gids(html)
      update_attachments(html) do |node|
        if (sgid = SignedGlobalID.parse(node["sgid"], for: ::ActionText::Attachable::LOCATOR_NAME))
          node["gid"] = URI::GID.build(app: sgid.app, model_name: sgid.model_name, model_id: sgid.model_id).to_s
        end

        node.remove_attribute("sgid")
      end
    end

    def import_batch(batch)
      rows = batch.map { |file| prepare(load(file)) }
      attachables = attachables_for(rows)

      rows.each do |row|
        row["body"] = convert_gids_to_sgids(row["body"], attachables)
      end

      insert_new rows
    end

    def attachables_for(rows)
      gids = rows.flat_map { |row| gids_in(row["body"]) }

      gids.group_by(&:model_name).flat_map do |model_name, gids_for_model|
        if (model = attachable_model_for(model_name))
          model.where(account: account, id: gids_for_model.map(&:model_id)).to_a
        else
          []
        end
      end.index_by { |attachable| [ attachable.class.polymorphic_name, attachable.id ] }
    end

    def gids_in(html)
      if html.present?
        ::ActionText::Fragment.wrap(html).find_all("#{ATTACHMENT_SELECTOR}[gid]").filter_map { |node| GlobalID.parse(node["gid"]) }
      else
        []
      end
    end

    def attachable_model_for(model_name)
      if (model = exportable_models[model_name]) && model.include?(::ActionText::Attachable)
        model
      end
    end

    def convert_gids_to_sgids(html, attachables)
      update_attachments(html) do |node|
        # Signed ids from elsewhere can't be trusted, and wouldn't verify anyway
        node.remove_attribute("sgid")

        if (gid = GlobalID.parse(node["gid"])) && (attachable = attachables[[ gid.model_name, gid.model_id ]])
          node["sgid"] = attachable.attachable_sgid
        end

        node.remove_attribute("gid")
      end
    end

    def update_attachments(html, &block)
      if html.present?
        ::ActionText::Fragment.wrap(html).update do |source|
          source.css(ATTACHMENT_SELECTOR).each(&block)
        end.to_html
      else
        html
      end
    end
end

messages.thinking:
I'm noting that MailDeliveryJob picks up account tenancy automatically, so the failure mail should be enqueued with `Current.without_account`, and since jobs wait for transaction commit, this needs to happen outside any open transaction. For the account export ready email, the context already has the account set correctly. Now I'm moving on to look at how the import cleanup method removes imported data.

For removing an account's data, I'm going through each model in the manifest in reverse order and batch-deleting rows by account_id, handling ActiveStorage blobs by deleting their files from the service before removing the records, and recognizing that search records are already handled via the account's destroy callback. I'm flagging a tricky issue though: HABTM join table rows for filters won't get cleaned up by a simple delete_all on filters, so I need a way to clear those join rows first, which may require giving each record set type its own removal logic since some override how records are scoped.

Alternatively, I'm weighing whether to just rely on `account.destroy`/`incinerate` and its dependent cascades, tracing through what actually gets destroyed that way—users, boards, cards, webhooks, tags, columns, and so on—and wondering whether notifications, events, mentions, reactions, filters, bundles, accesses, pins, and watches are all covered by nested dependent associations. The tradeoff is that full cascading destroy callbacks could be slow for large imports, but correctness matters more, except I'm worried those callbacks might choke on inconsistent imported data.

The bigger concern is that per-record destroy callbacks that enqueue broadcast or search-removal jobs would flood the job queue at scale, whereas a bulk sweep using `delete_all` across the manifest models and join tables is fast and clean, as long as it covers everything—identities, files, search records, storage entries—leaving `account.destroy` to handle the remaining account-level cleanup like the join code, entropy, search records, storage totals, and the import record's zip attachment purge.

I'm now worried the zip attachment's purge job might fail since it runs with `Current.account` set to the account being destroyed, so by the time it executes the account may already be gone, causing a DeserializationError and silently leaving the file undeleted. I check whether `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` inherits account-tenancy and confirm it doesn't, since it's not an `ApplicationJob` subclass, so that job runs fine with just a blob GlobalID. But to be safe for the import's zip file specifically, I think the cleanup should purge it synchronously rather than relying on the async job.

I'm sketching the cleanup method: scoping to the account, purging the zip file synchronously, then walking the manifest's record sets in reverse order to delete them, removing created identities, and finally incinerating the account with storage-deletion callbacks suppressed. I'm debating what to call the record-set deletion method — `delete_imported`, `clear`, or just `delete_all` — and I settle on `delete_all` for consistency with ActiveRecord naming, implemented as a batched `where(account_id:).delete_all` without callbacks.

For `FileRecordSet#delete_all`, I need to actually delete the underlying blob files in storage before the blob rows themselves get deleted — since manifest order puts files last, reversing it naturally deletes files first. I'm confirming that `Blob#delete` already handles both the primary file and any prefixed variant files for image blobs, so I can just call that for each blob in the account.

Double-checking: scoping by `account_id` means I'll never touch another account's blobs, and since blob keys are unique across the whole DB, there's no risk of accidentally deleting a file that happens to share a key with another account.

For the other record sets, filters need their join rows deleted before the filters themselves, the account record set is a no-op since the account gets destroyed separately, and users just get deleted outright along with any placeholder users. For identities, I'm narrowing to emails from the imported users, created after the import started, with no attached users, to avoid wiping out identities that existed independently.

Destroying matching identities should cascade cleanly through their access tokens, magic links, sessions, and avatar, but I want to guard against accidentally deleting a real person's pending signup by also requiring no sessions and no magic links exist. Since identities are only created during the finalize/link_identities step, I'm deciding it's simplest to just always run this cleanup against the zip's email list regardless of which stage failed, since it's cheap and will naturally be a no-op if finalize never ran.

That approach is simple and robust — collect emails before purging the file. For failure handling: ConflictError only deletes our account's rows, leaving conflicting ones untouched, with no identities created in that case; IntegrityError and ZipFile::InvalidFileError get user-facing messages while other errors get a generic "something went wrong" message to avoid leaking internals. Now I'm drafting the ImportMailer's completed notification, sent to the identity's email with a subject line about the import finishing.

Now I'm working out the failed mailer method signature and its message, then moving on to the Export classes, checking attachment record types across the STI hierarchy for Export and Account::Import, and sketching the has_one_attached setup for Export's file.

I'm also verifying blob account defaulting via Current.account for both S3 direct uploads and controller-created imports, then starting to write the zip population logic for the user's data export by iterating over exportable cards.

Now I'm working out how to define `exportable_cards` — needing to combine published cards with drafted cards created by the user across their accessible boards, since `accessible_cards` is a has_many-through relation and combining it with `.or` requires building an equivalent query directly on `Card`.

I'm sketching out a `Card::Exportable` concern to handle generating the JSON export and gathering attachments for a card...

Still designing export fields...

I'm figuring out the rest of the JSON structure: tags, assignees, steps, creator, description with both plain text and HTML versions, image, attachments with metadata, timestamps, and nested comments each with their own creator, body, attachments, and timestamps, plus a shared person shape for name and email. For description_html, I'm considering how to render the rich text body so embedded attachments resolve to relative file paths instead of action-text tags.

I need to look at how render_attachments works -- it replaces each attachment node with a block result, so I'm planning for blob attachables to become links or images depending on type, mentions to become plain @name text, and everything else to fall back to a plain representation before converting to HTML. I want to check the actual implementation to get the details right.

# A ZIP archive of data built in the background for someone to download. The
# download link is emailed when it's ready, and works for a day.
class Export < ApplicationRecord
  DOWNLOAD_PERIOD = 1.day
  DAILY_LIMIT = 10

  belongs_to :account
  belongs_to :user

  has_one_attached :file, dependent: :purge_later

  enum :status, %w[ pending processing completed failed ].index_by(&:itself), default: :pending

  scope :current, -> { where(created_at: DOWNLOAD_PERIOD.ago..) }
  scope :in_progress, -> { where(status: %w[ pending processing ]) }
  scope :expired, -> { where(completed_at: ...DOWNLOAD_PERIOD.ago).or(where(status: %w[ pending processing failed ], created_at: ...DOWNLOAD_PERIOD.ago)) }

  class << self
    def cleanup
      expired.find_each(&:destroy)
    end

    def limit_reached_for?(user)
      where(user: user).current.count >= DAILY_LIMIT
    end
  end

  def build_later
    DataExportJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def build
    processing!

    with_context do
      ZipFile.create_for(file, filename: filename) do |zip|
        populate_zip(zip)
      end

      mark_completed
      ExportMailer.completed(self).deliver_later
    end
  rescue => error
    failed!
    raise error
  end

  def mark_completed
    update!(status: :completed, completed_at: Time.current)
  end

  def expires_at
    completed_at + DOWNLOAD_PERIOD if completed_at
  end

  def expired?
    expires_at&.past?
  end

  def downloadable?
    completed? && !expired? && file.attached?
  end

  def accessible_to?(accessor)
    accessor.present? && accessor == user && downloadable?
  end

  private
    def with_context
      Current.set(account: account, user: user) { yield }
    end

    def filename
      "#{filename_prefix.parameterize.presence || "fizzy"}-#{created_at.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")}.zip"
    end

    def filename_prefix
      raise NotImplementedError, "Subclasses must implement filename_prefix"
    end

    def populate_zip(zip)
      raise NotImplementedError, "Subclasses must implement populate_zip"
    end
end

# The JSON representation of a card in personal data exports, with its comments
# and every file attached to it. Files are referenced by their path in the
# export, next to the card's JSON file.
module Card::Exportable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  ExportedAttachment = Data.define(:path, :blob)

  def export_json
    JSON.pretty_generate(export_data)
  end

  def export_attachments
    @export_attachments ||= begin
      paths = Set.new

      exportable_blobs.uniq(&:id).map do |blob|
        ExportedAttachment.new(path: unique_export_path_for(blob, paths), blob: blob)
      end
    end
  end

  private
    def export_data
      {
        number: number,
        title: title,
        board: board.name,
        column: column&.name,
        status: status,
        closed: closed?,
        closed_at: closure&.created_at&.utc&.iso8601,
        closed_by: export_person(closure&.user),
        postponed: postponed?,
        golden: golden?,
        due_on: due_on&.iso8601,
        tags: tags.map(&:title).sort,
        creator: export_person(creator),
        assignees: assignees.map { |assignee| export_person(assignee) },
        steps: steps.map { |step| { content: step.content, completed: step.completed? } },
        description: description.to_plain_text,
        description_html: export_html(description.body),
        image: image.attached? ? export_path_for(image.blob) : nil,
        attachments: export_attachments_for(description.embeds),
        created_at: created_at.utc.iso8601,
        updated_at: updated_at.utc.iso8601,
        last_active_at: last_active_at.utc.iso8601,
        comments: comments.sort_by(&:created_at).map { |comment| export_comment(comment) }
      }
    end

    def export_comment(comment)
      {
        id: comment.id,
        creator: export_person(comment.creator),
        body: comment.body.to_plain_text,
        body_html: export_html(comment.body.body),
        attachments: export_attachments_for(comment.body.embeds),
        created_at: comment.created_at.utc.iso8601,
        updated_at: comment.updated_at.utc.iso8601
      }
    end

    def export_person(user)
      { name: user.name, email_address: user.identity&.email_address } if user
    end

    def export_attachments_for(attachments)
      attachments.map do |attachment|
        {
          filename: attachment.filename.to_s,
          content_type: attachment.content_type,
          byte_size: attachment.byte_size,
          path: export_path_for(attachment.blob)
        }
      end
    end

    # Rich text with its attachments pointing at the files in the export.
    def export_html(content)
      if content.present?
        content.render_attachments do |attachment|
          export_html_for_attachment(attachment)
        end.to_html
      end
    end

    def export_html_for_attachment(attachment)
      attachable = attachment.attachable

      if attachable.is_a?(ActiveStorage::Blob) && (path = export_path_for(attachable))
        if attachable.image?
          ApplicationController.helpers.image_tag(path, alt: attachable.filename.to_s)
        else
          ApplicationController.helpers.link_to(attachable.filename.to_s, path)
        end
      else
        ERB::Util.html_escape(attachment.to_plain_text)
      end
    end

    def exportable_blobs
      [ image.attached? ? image.blob : nil, *description.embeds.map(&:blob), *comments.flat_map { |comment| comment.body.embeds.map(&:blob) } ].compact
    end

    def export_path_for(blob)
      export_attachments.find { |attachment| attachment.blob.id == blob.id }&.path
    end

    def unique_export_path_for(blob, paths)
      filename = blob.filename.sanitized
      base, extension = File.basename(filename, ".*"), File.extname(filename)

      candidates = Enumerator.produce(1, &:succ).lazy.map do |count|
        "#{number}/#{count == 1 ? base : "#{base} (#{count})"}#{extension}"
      end

      candidates.find { |path| paths.add?(path) }
    end
end

# Brings an account export into the new account it was created for.
#
# The whole file is checked before anything gets imported. If the import can't
# be completed, everything it brought in goes away along with the account, and
# the person who started it gets an email saying why.
class Account::Import < ApplicationRecord
  STAGES = %w[ check import finalize ].freeze
  GENERIC_FAILURE_REASON = "Something went wrong while importing the file.".freeze

  belongs_to :account
  belongs_to :identity

  has_one_attached :file, dependent: :purge_later

  enum :status, %w[ pending processing completed failed ].index_by(&:itself), default: :pending

  scope :in_progress, -> { where(status: %w[ pending processing ]) }

  def process_later
    ImportAccountDataJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  # Imports the file. Yields a cursor as it makes progress, which can be passed
  # back as +start+ to resume an interrupted import.
  def process(start: nil, &checkpoint)
    stage, record_set_index, offset = start.presence || [ STAGES.first, 0, 0 ]

    processing! unless processing?

    ZipFile.read_from(file.blob) do |zip|
      Current.with_account(account) do
        if stage == "check"
          check(zip, record_set_index, offset, &checkpoint)
          record_set_index, offset = 0, 0
        end

        if stage.in?(%w[ check import ])
          import(zip, record_set_index, offset, &checkpoint)
        end

        checkpoint&.call([ "finalize", 0, 0 ])
        finalize(zip)
      end
    end

    mark_completed
  rescue => error
    mark_failed(error)
    raise error
  end

  private
    def check(zip, record_set_index, offset, &checkpoint)
      each_record_set(record_set_index, offset) do |record_set, index, start|
        record_set.check(from: zip, start: start) do |checked|
          checkpoint&.call([ "check", index, checked ])
        end
      end
    end

    def import(zip, record_set_index, offset, &checkpoint)
      each_record_set(record_set_index, offset) do |record_set, index, start|
        record_set.import(from: zip, start: start) do |imported|
          checkpoint&.call([ "import", index, imported ])
        end
      end
    end

    def each_record_set(record_set_index, offset)
      manifest.each_record_set(start: record_set_index) do |record_set, index|
        yield record_set, index, (index == record_set_index ? offset : 0)
      end
    end

    def manifest
      @manifest ||= Account::DataTransfer::Manifest.new(account)
    end

    def finalize(zip)
      remove_replaced_system_users(zip)
      Account::DataTransfer::UserRecordSet.new(account).link_identities(from: zip)
      make_importer_the_owner
      reindex_for_search
      reconcile_storage
    end

    # Accounts come with a system user, but the export brings its own.
    def remove_replaced_system_users(zip)
      users = Account::DataTransfer::UserRecordSet.new(account)
      system_users = account.users.where(role: :system).to_a

      if system_users.any? { |user| users.exported?(user, from: zip) }
        system_users.reject { |user| users.exported?(user, from: zip) }.each(&:destroy!)
      end
    end

    # Whoever imports the account owns it, and gets to see everything in it.
    def make_importer_the_owner
      importer = account.users.find_by!(identity: identity)

      account.users.where(role: :owner).where.not(id: importer.id).update_all(role: :admin)
      importer.update!(role: :owner, active: true, verified_at: importer.verified_at || Time.current)

      grant_access_to_every_board(importer)
    end

    def grant_access_to_every_board(user)
      board_ids = account.boards.where.not(id: user.accesses.select(:board_id)).ids

      if board_ids.any?
        Access.insert_all! board_ids.map { |board_id| { id: ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid.generate, account_id: account.id, board_id: board_id, user_id: user.id } }
      end
    end

    def reindex_for_search
      account.cards.includes(:rich_text_description).find_each(&:reindex)
      Comment.where(account: account).includes(:card, :rich_text_body).find_each(&:reindex)
    end

    def reconcile_storage
      Storage::ReconcileJob.perform_later(account)
      account.boards.find_each { |board| Storage::ReconcileJob.perform_later(board) }
    end

    def mark_completed
      update!(status: :completed, completed_at: Time.current)
      file.purge_later

      ImportMailer.completed(self).deliver_later
    end

    def mark_failed(error)
      failed!
      notify_failure(error)
      remove_imported_data
    end

    def notify_failure(error)
      reason = failure_reason_for(error)

      # The account is about to be removed, so the email can't depend on it
      Current.without_account do
        ImportMailer.failed(identity, reason: reason).deliver_later
      end
    end

    def failure_reason_for(error)
      case error
      when Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet::IntegrityError, ZipFile::Error
        error.message
      else
        Rails.error.report(error, context: { account_import_id: id })
        GENERIC_FAILURE_REASON
      end
    end

    # Leaves nothing behind: imported records and files, people created for the
    # import, the uploaded file and the account itself.
    def remove_imported_data
      email_addresses = imported_email_addresses

      file.purge if file.attached?
      manifest.record_sets.reverse_each(&:delete_all)
      remove_identities_created_for(email_addresses)
      account.incinerate
    end

    def imported_email_addresses
      ZipFile.read_from(file.blob) do |zip|
        Account::DataTransfer::UserRecordSet.new(account).email_addresses(from: zip)
      end
    rescue ZipFile::Error, Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet::IntegrityError, ActiveStorage::FileNotFoundError
      []
    end

    def remove_identities_created_for(email_addresses)
      Identity.where(email_address: email_addresses, created_at: created_at..)
        .where.not(id: identity_id)
        .where.missing(:users, :sessions, :magic_links, :access_tokens)
        .find_each(&:destroy!)
    end
end

# Imports can take hours for large accounts, so they make progress across
# restarts: an interrupted import resumes from its last checkpoint.
class ImportAccountDataJob < ApplicationJob
  include ActiveJob::Continuable

  queue_as :backend

  # A failed import has already been cleaned up, so there's nothing to resume.
  self.resume_errors_after_advancing = false

  discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError

  # Problems with the file itself are reported to whoever started the import.
  discard_on Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet::IntegrityError, ZipFile::Error

  def perform(import)
    step :process do |step|
      import.process(start: step.cursor) do |cursor|
        step.set! cursor
      end
    end
  end
end

  end

        import = start_import(signup.account)
        redirect_to account_import_path(import, script_name: signup.account.slug)
      else
        redirect_to new_account_import_path, alert: signup.errors.full_messages.to_sentence

      if file.respond_to?(:read)
        file.read(2) == "PK".b

module DataTransferTestHelper
  private
    def export_account(account, user: account.users.admin.first)
      Account::Export.create!(account: account, user: user).tap(&:build)
    end

    def exported_zip(export)
      export.file.download
    end

    def create_import(zip, identity:)
      signup = Signup.new(identity: identity, full_name: identity.email_address.split("@").first, skip_account_seeding: true)
      assert signup.complete, signup.errors.full_messages.to_sentence

      Current.with_account(signup.account) do
        signup.account.imports.create!(identity: identity, file: { io: StringIO.new(zip), filename: "export.zip", content_type: "application/zip" })
      end
    end

    def build_zip
      tempfile = Tempfile.new([ "test", ".zip" ], binmode: true)
      writer = ZipFile::Writer.new(tempfile)
      yield writer
      writer.close
      tempfile.rewind
      tempfile.read
    ensure
      tempfile&.close!
    end

    def with_zip_reader(zip)
      Tempfile.create([ "test", ".zip" ], binmode: true) do |tempfile|
        tempfile.write(zip)
        tempfile.rewind
        yield ZipFile::Reader.new(tempfile)
      end
    end

    # Rewrites some files in an archive, keeping everything else as it was.
    def rewrite_zip(zip)
      with_zip_reader(zip) do |reader|
        build_zip do |writer|
          reader.glob("**/*").each do |path|
            content = reader.read(path)
            writer.add_file(path, yield(path, content) || content)
          end
        end
      end
    end
end
EOF

I realize `assert_enqueued_email_with` needs ActionMailer::TestHelper included in the test class since it's not part of ActiveSupport::TestCase by default. I'm also noticing a round trip conflict where blobs still exist after `@source.incinerate` — account destroy isn't cleaning up blobs that aren't attached, or the purge_later flow for attachments isn't completing synchronously.

Tracing through: destroying an account destroys its attachments, which calls purge_later and enqueues jobs that aren't performed in tests, so blobs linger and cause conflicts. Even in production, truly orphaned blobs (never attached, or left behind from a different account) would never get purged by incineration, meaning re-importing into the same instance could hit permanent primary-key conflicts — I'm weighing whether conflict detection should special-case blobs belonging to accounts that no longer exist, though deleting orphaned blobs automatically feels risky.

In the test itself, the fix is straightforward: wrap `@source.incinerate` in `perform_enqueued_jobs(only: ActiveStorage::PurgeJob)` so purge actually runs before checking for conflicts, since our overridden job helper already resets `Current.account` to nil safely.

But I want to keep this narrowly scoped to blobs specifically, since they're the one record type guaranteed to outlive their account due to `purge_later`, rather than generalizing the non-existent-account skip to all record types.

Actually this is a nasty race condition: if a purge job for an account's blobs runs after import inserts new rows with the same id/key, GlobalID deserialization would find and destroy the freshly imported blob instead of the old one, causing real data loss. Without deleting leftovers first, the conflict check would instead block import until pending purge jobs complete.
